text:
Help me write a case for my promotion. I'm the assistant front office manager at a 180-room hotel, and the front office manager job is open. I'm applying, and my general manager wants it in writing by Friday.

Facts:
- I've worked here 6 years, the last 2 as assistant manager.
- Our guest score for check-in on the main review site went from 7.9 to 8.6 over the last 18 months. The lobby and all the rooms were renovated during the same time.
- I rewrote the front desk training. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9.
- Front desk turnover was 9 of 14 people in the year before I became assistant manager, and 5 of 14 last year.
- I've covered the front office manager's job alone for the 7 weeks since she left.
- I have never managed a budget. The front office manager owns a $1.1 million payroll budget.

I want it to say I'm the main reason our guest scores went up. One page.

Before I draft, here's how I'd build the case, one claim I'd advise against, and a few questions.

**The argument as I see it**

- **Claim:** You should be the next front office manager.
- **Grounds:**
  - You've effectively been doing the job alone for 7 weeks.
  - Front desk turnover fell from 64% (9 of 14) to 36% (5 of 14).
  - New hires now work the desk alone in 5 shifts instead of 9, about 45% faster.
  - The check-in score rose from 7.9 to 8.6.
  - You've been at the hotel 6 years.
- **Link between the two:** The best predictor of how someone will do the job is how they've already done it, and you've done it.
- **Main objection:** "You've never managed a budget, and this job owns $1.1M in payroll."
- **Second objection:** "The scores went up because we renovated."

**The "main reason" claim**

Your GM approved the renovation and knows when it happened. If the page says you're the main reason scores rose, the GM will probably think "the new lobby" straight away. That doubt then spreads to the claims that are solid: turnover, training and the 7 weeks. Your facts show the score rose while you rebuilt the desk. They don't show how much of the rise was yours and how much was the renovation.

A version your facts do support: *"The renovation gave guests a better lobby. The training and a steadier team gave them a better check-in. Check-in is the part of the stay my desk controls, and it went from 7.9 to 8.6."* That still gives you real credit, and the turnover and training numbers back it up. If you can answer question 2 below, we may be able to say more. It's your call, and I'll write whichever version you choose.

**Questions (the first matters most)**

1. **Budget.** Over the 7 weeks, have you made scheduling, staffing or overtime decisions? Are there any labor numbers, like overtime hours or labor cost per occupied room, that stayed on target or improved? And what would you commit to on the budget? For example, working through the first budget cycle with the GM or controller. This is the objection the GM will certainly raise, so the page needs an answer to it.
2. **Score timing.** Do you have monthly or quarterly check-in scores showing when the rise happened compared with when your training started and when the renovation finished? Do any reviews mention staff by name or talk about fast or friendly check-in? Either would let us claim more credit.
3. **Training rollout.** When did the new training start, and how many hires have gone through it?
4. **The 7 weeks.** Anything specific from that time? A problem you handled, a number that held steady, or something the GM said about how it's gone.
5. **Details.** The GM's name, your name as it should appear, and whether this goes as a memo or a letter.

Answer whatever you can. Anything you leave out, I'll leave out rather than guess.

Fair point on "main reason." I'm fine with your version that says what I did.

1. In the 7 weeks, no front desk shift went uncovered and overtime came in under the monthly plan. I don't have labor cost per occupied room. On the budget, I can commit to finishing the company's finance course in my first 3 months (the company pays for it), and to weekly sessions on the payroll budget with our controller, Ben Oduya. He's already offered.

2. The renovation started 5 months into the 18 months. Check-in had already gone from 7.9 to 8.2 before it started. I don't know if any reviews mention staff by name.

3. I don't know the exact start date or how many hires have gone through it.

4. Just the shift coverage and overtime above. Nothing from the GM that I can point to.

5. I'm Daniela Ruiz. The GM is Mark Ellison. Memo or letter, whichever you think works better.

I've written it as a memo. That suits an internal application your GM asked for in writing. It runs about 380 words, so it fits on one page.

<final_document>
**MEMO**

**To:** Mark Ellison, General Manager
**From:** Daniela Ruiz, Assistant Front Office Manager
**Re:** Application for Front Office Manager

I'm applying for the front office manager position. For the last seven weeks I have done this job on my own, and I'd like to keep doing it with the title and responsibility that go with it.

**The last seven weeks**

Since the position opened, every front desk shift has been covered, and overtime has come in under the monthly plan. That wasn't a trial run. It was the job, and you've seen how it has gone.

**What I've built in two years as assistant manager**

- **A team that stays.** In the year before I became assistant manager, 9 of our 14 front desk staff left. Last year, 5 did. Turnover went from 64% to 36%.
- **Faster training.** I rewrote the front desk training. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9, which cuts nearly half the time before they can carry a shift.
- **Better check-ins.** Our check-in score on the main review site rose from 7.9 to 8.6 over the last 18 months. The renovation helped, because guests notice a new lobby. But check-in is the part of the stay the front desk controls, and the score had already risen from 7.9 to 8.2 in the five months before the renovation began.

**The budget**

I haven't managed a budget, and this role owns a $1.1 million payroll. Here is how I will close that gap:

- I will complete the company's finance course within my first three months.
- I will meet weekly with Ben Oduya on the payroll budget. He has already offered to work with me.

The payroll budget is mostly scheduling and overtime. Those are the decisions I've been making for the last seven weeks, and overtime has stayed under plan.

**Why me**

I've worked at this hotel for six years. The team I would manage is the team I trained, using training I wrote. Someone from outside would first have to learn the hotel, the staff and the systems already in place, and the desk would be in transition again while they did. I can keep it running the way it has run for the past seven weeks, and keep improving it.

I'd welcome the chance to talk this through with you before you decide.

Daniela Ruiz
</parameter>
</final_document>

A few notes:

- **The scores:** the strongest point you have is that check-in rose from 7.9 to 8.2 before the renovation started. That's why the memo can admit the renovation helped and still give your desk real credit. Your GM can check those dates.
- **Not in the memo:** I didn't say when your training started or that it caused the early rise, because you don't know the start date. If you can find it and it's before the renovation, add one line: "The new training was in place by [month]."
- **Worth a quick look before Friday:** if any reviews from the last 18 months mention desk staff by name or say check-in was fast, one short quote would strengthen the check-in section.
- **Date:** I left the date line off. Add it when you send the memo.
